In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the currently accepted radical pathway remains the most likely mechanistic pathway, but the carbocation mechanism remains a possibility.

the peroxide bond in both artemisinin and its derivatives is not likely to be the site of protonation and subsequent cleavage to a carbocation, and therefore the radical pathway remains the most likely explanation for antimalarials activity.
artemisinin and its derivatives are not activated in acidic media to give carbocations at C4 and therefore the ionic mechanism is not a viable alternative to the radical mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antimalarials are stable to acid and that the preferred site of protonation is the O5a oxygen in artemisinin and O4a oxygen in arteether.
the peroxide bond is too stable in artemisinin and the ether bond in arteether to be readily cleaved by protonation and therefore the radical pathway is the likeliest mode of action.
the trioxanes are stable under acidic conditions and that the most probable site for acid catalysed decomposition is the C4-C5 bond.
The main takeaway from our work is that
arteether is more susceptible to acid catalysed decomposition than artemisinin.
artemisinin and related trioxanes are not stable in acidic conditions and that this may be relevant in vivo, particularly in acidic tissues.
the peroxide bond in both artemisinin and artether is not a likely site for protonation and therefore the carbocation mechanism is unlikely.
